soundcheck.heard: Landslides have killed people in Southeast Alaska, and now a university plans a computer copy of a hillside that keeps up. Can that cartoon keep up with a real mountain? According to the NSF award record, the University of Alaska Fairbanks gets $1.77 million over six years. Carl Tape is the principal investigator, and the aim is a digital twin, a stand-in for a real slope. Slopes fail in a chain, the award abstract says. Rain soaks the hill, a quake weakens it, a later storm brings it down. Haynes, December 2020. At least eight inches of rain in two days per the news outlet, KHNS, and two people killed. Rangle, November 2023. A landslide killed six. The plan pulls in ground shaking, satellite pictures, weather and groundwater, which the abstract says come from separate systems that rarely work together. So it would add fast surrogate models, quick stand-ins for slow physics, tugged closer to the slope by each new reading. Now the fair case. Nothing is built, and the award record is the only public source. The University of Washington holds a larger part of the award, and testing is planned with no results. A loop only sharpens where instruments exist, so it could keep up where there are sensors, and nowhere else. The award names no Alaska slope. Barry Arm is one state geologist's track, roughly 500 million cubic meters, and a fast failure could make a tsunami with life-threatening waves. Which slope would the twin learn first? Nobody said. Which would you pick?
